• Common name: Brazilian pennywort
  • Other names: Mushroom pennywort, moneywort, Brazilian water-ivy
  • Scientific name: Hydrocotyle leucocephala
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Difficulty: easy
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Optimal pH: 6.0–8.0
  • Water hardness: soft to hard (4–18 GH)
  • Temperature: 22–28°C
  • Substrate: any
  • Can float: yes
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Placement in tank: midground / background
  • Fertilizer: recommended
  • CO2: not needed, but recommended when submersed
  • Propagation: by clipping mature stems or lateral shoots

Hydrocotyle leucocephala is a versatile freshwater aquarium plant of the genus Hydrocotyle, which contains about 100+ species of perennial, aquatic or semi-aquatic plants.

Hydrocotyle comes from the Greek words "hydro" (water) and "kotyle" (dish/plate), hinting at the shape of the leaves. The species name leucocephala is also of Greek origin: leuc means "white" and cephal means "head", referring to the whitish flowers arranged in heads or clusters.

This stem plant grows in boggy areas in Central and South America. It has long, bright green, vine-like foliage.

It is native to Central and South America, occurring in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Venezuela and southern Mexico.
In the wild it grows in wetlands, bogs, marshes, and still or slow-moving rivers.

The recommended minimum tank size is 40 litres. It is not a good idea to keep it in smaller tanks unless you are ready to trim it frequently, since it grows very rapidly. It always grows towards the surface.

Hydrocotyle leucocephala is one of the easiest plants to maintain in a freshwater planted tank. It is hardy and has minimal demands.

Pruning is the major care task because the plant grows quite fast. Under optimal conditions it can overrun the tank if left untrimmed. Prune excess growth and dispose of the shoots properly, and nip off browning or pale stems and leaves. To fill sparse areas, you can introduce some cuttings.

The frequency of pruning depends on how fast the plant grows (especially with fertilizers and CO2); you may need to cut it every week. Be careful not to tug or damage healthy shoots.

Fertilizers, mainly those rich in macronutrients and iron, are essential to prevent deficiencies such as yellowing leaves, so add fertilizer after every significant partial water change. Partial water changes also promote excellent water quality. The plant removes a great deal of nitrate by absorbing nutrients, but not necessarily down to ideal levels, so regular water changes are needed to lower it further.

Planting and propagation

As a floating plant (it actually does better this way): divide the plant, disinfect the stems thoroughly and spread them on the water surface.

Alternatively, grow it in the substrate as a midground or background plant to add depth to the aquascape. Place healthy stems directly into the substrate (about 2.5–4 cm deep). The plant has small roots, which makes it very hard to keep planted, and placing it too deep can make it rot.

It can also accentuate décor (driftwood, bogwood, caves) if weighed down properly.

Propagation is easy: take cuttings from healthy mature stems or lateral shoots and replant them in the substrate or float them on the water. Within a week or two the cuttings sprout plenty of roots and growth explodes.

  • Grows slower when underwater
  • Requires a lot of light
  • Absorbs nutrients from the water

Problems

  • Melting: often occurs in stem plants after being moved from emersed to submersed conditions. It is normal for a plant grown on land to die back and shed some leaves; after a while it adapts and grows new leaves.
  • Melting after a few months: some aquarists report that after 5–6 months of amazing growth, the plant starts to gradually degrade. Solution: it does not like being fully submerged all the time and thrives in paludarium setups.
  • Sparse growth: usually caused by low light or a lack of essential nutrients. Solution: increase light intensity/photoperiod, dose fertilizers regularly and prune from time to time to encourage horizontal growth of shoots.
  • Balling: if you do not trim the floating plant, the current will push it into a ball and it will look like a giant mass over the tank. Solution: regular pruning.
  • Overgrowth: it can overrun the tank, shade and block light from plants at lower levels. Solution: prune excess foliage frequently.
  • Slow growth: caused by low light, very soft water or insufficient nutrients. Solution: make sure the water is not too soft, increase lighting, dose fertilizers and supply enough CO2. Check nitrate: the plant needs nitrate (>10).
  • Crooked roots: a sign of phosphorus deficiency, which this plant shows before other plants. Solution: add some phosphate.
  • Yellowing leaves: when parts (mainly the edges) turn yellow, it often indicates iron deficiency. Solution: provide chelated iron at the right dosage.

Temperature: the ideal temperature is 22–28°C. The plant needs warmer temperatures for optimal growth; lower temperatures slow its growth.

pH: 6.0–8.0 is required for optimal growth and health.

Hardness: the plant adapts to a range of water hardness values, but grows best in freshwater with a hardness of 4–18 GH.

Water flow: keeping it as a free-floating plant requires gentle surface agitation. Otherwise it will turn into a huge "balling" mess.

CO2 and fertilization: although it can do without CO2 supplementation, optimal growth is almost certain when the water is supplemented with pressurized or liquid carbon, which shows in the growth rate and in a lusher, healthier appearance. As a floater, the plant does not need additional CO2 dosing, as it gets enough from the air.

Fertilizers make the plant grow bushier and quicker. It is mostly a water column feeder: its root system is weak and it absorbs nutrients primarily through its leaves, so dose liquid fertilizers, not root tabs.

If you keep shrimp in the tank, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (which most fertilizers contain) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Lighting: the plant can grow even in dim light, but intense lighting is required to maintain its typical fast growth and robust appearance. Provide moderate-high lighting (30–50 PAR) with a high-quality LED light, and a standard photoperiod of at least 8 hours daily.

Substrate: it does not develop an extensive root system and prefers to float, with its leaves growing emersed. There is no need for a nutrient-rich substrate; it can grow anywhere, including sand and gravel.

Brazilian pennywort is characterized by its relatively small (around 2.5–3 cm), round, flat, vibrant green leaves (resembling lily pads) borne on thin green stalks. The plant also has upright/creeping stems, fine, delicate, stringy white roots, and small, whitish flowers (seen in emersed plants).

It is a fast-growing aquarium plant. It can grow up to 60 cm in height and about 15 cm in width under optimal conditions.

Due to its attractive, vine or ivy-like appearance, it is a great fit for paludarium setups. It is also quite versatile: it can be grown in any substrate as a midground or background plant, or left floating on the water surface. Some people keep it as a foreground plant, but it is time-consuming to keep it along the substrate.

It is also ideal for removing excess nitrates from the aquarium water. Its roots (when floating) serve as a haven for fish fry and a good medium for infusoria to grow.

The plant is overall light green, and its colour is more pronounced when grown in well-lit tanks with ample nutrient supply.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: its shape and chaotic form make an excellent decorative addition to a jungle aquascape.
  • Versatility: one of a few plants that look good as a background plant, a floating plant, or even in emersed/terrestrial form.
  • Removal of excess nutrients: it depends heavily on nutrients in the water column, so it helps with nitrate, ammonia and phosphate problems. It can be used as an indicator of nutrient levels: when the leaves start to lighten up, it does not have enough nutrition.
  • Firmness: it does not shed leaves as many other floaters do.
  • Replacement: even if rooted, it can be easily moved or removed. Its roots are very thin and delicate, so you will not pull up a big part of the substrate with it.
  • Hiding place: serves as cover and shade for invertebrates and small fish, and is a perfect hiding place for shrimp and fish.
  • Foraging place: acts as a buffet of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Oxygenation: it oxygenates and aerates the tank water.

Compatible tankmates

  • Fish: for example bettas, swordtails, tetras, pearl gourami, honey gourami, harlequin rasbora, danios, cherry barbs, platies, guppies, Endlers, mollies, otocinclus catfish, pygmy cory catfish, etc.
  • Snails: for example Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.
  • Dwarf shrimp: all varieties of Neocaridina (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Snowball, Black Rose, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Rili, etc.) or Caridina species (for example Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger), Amano shrimp, ghost shrimp, bamboo shrimp, vampire shrimp. Basically any shrimp species can be kept with it.

Avoid keeping goldfish, silver dollars, Oscars, Jack Dempsey, koi and Buenos Aires tetra, since they will devour the foliage. The same goes for large, aggressive fish such as cichlids, which can tear the plant, damage the stems and dislodge its roots.

Unless you keep it as a floating plant, do not keep it with most crayfish or freshwater crabs, which will cut, eat and uproot everything in the tank.

Buying

It is readily available at local fish stores, online stores or from hobbyists willing to spare a few stems. A pot or bunch usually contains 2–4 stems, so you may need more than 2 pots, depending on the size of the aquarium and how you intend to grow it.

Look for healthy specimens with vibrant green stems and leaves, free of rips, holes and discolouration, with abundant white roots. Do not buy specimens with broken stems, torn/discoloured/curled leaves or dark brown roots.

Quarantine

Unless you are completely sure the plant is safe (for example grown in vitro and the in vitro pot is undamaged and unopened), quarantine and disinfect it to avoid contamination.

  • The plant can carry parasites and hitchhikers such as pest snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It could also have been treated with chemicals (pesticides) to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

Brazilian pennywort is well suited to adorning the midground or background of an aquarium. It is loved for its bright green foliage, ease of care and ability to remove excess nitrates. Some people also use the leaves in dishes because of their slight peppery taste. It is easy to plant, propagate and care for, and is recommended for beginners.
